results: Each member benchmarked a different part of the pipeline, and every run was scored with the team's shared scorer: exact match of RDKit canonical SMILES (RDKit 2026.3.2) against the answer key, the sponsor paper's rule (Gulluoglu et al., 2026). Will ran the MolDetV2 detector, the MolScribe and MolGlyph readers, and full BioMiner; Jin ran MolSight; Peter ran MolNexTR and MolGlyph on older sets; Bijay ran DECIMER, MolGrapher, and DeepSeek-OCR-2 (Adranly, 2026; Chhetri, 2026; Daly, 2026; Jin, 2026). The data were BioVista's 8,006 test crops from journal figures (Yan et al., 2026), the 2,482 molecule crops on Patent300's 300 patent pages (LG AI Research, 2025), and the six internal papers (220 molecules) as whole PDFs. The tables are generated from files committed to the group repository (XN Project Group 1, 2026b).

On Patent300 pages, MolDetV2 found 99.4% of molecules at 99.7% precision (Daly, 2026). For comparison, the sponsor paper's Claude Code pipeline found 13 of the 220 (Gulluoglu et al., 2026).

analysis: Where two members measured the same thing, they agree, so you can compare their numbers directly. Peter's and Will's MolGlyph setups were built independently, Peter's on a GPU through BioMiner's own code and Will's on a laptop CPU. Yet they read the same 790 of 1,000 BioVista crops correctly, crop for crop, and both land within about two points of the 76.4% BioMiner's authors publish (Adranly, 2026; Daly, 2026; Yan et al., 2026). Jin's MolSight run reused Will's 233 MolDetV2 boxes, and Will's GPU and CPU MolScribe runs matched exactly, so the reader differences in Table 3 come from the readers, not from hardware or cropping (Jin, 2026). The one source of run-to-run noise we found is MolGlyph's GPU batching inside BioMiner, which changed 2 of 8 readings on paper 16.

The largest discrepancies between members came from how R-groups are written, not from how drawings are read. Peter's scorer gave MolGlyph 76.0% on his BioVista sample and 0 of 23 Markush structures on CLEF and JPO; the team scorer, which treats the R-group labels [1*] and * as the same atom, gives 79.0% on the same BioVista crops (Adranly, 2026). Bijay's three readers scored exactly 0% on 3,596 Markush crops because none of them write * at all, although their Tanimoto similarity on those crops (0.25 to 0.43) shows they read part of each structure (Chhetri, 2026). Rewriting each reader's own placeholder as * before scoring (rules fixed on BioVista's validation split; Bijay's rescoring of the committed predictions) raises DECIMER's Markush accuracy from 0% to 17.0% and MolGrapher's to 1.8%, and leaves DeepSeek-OCR-2 at 0%, far below MolGlyph's 82.0%. A Markush score measures output notation as much as recognition, so one convention has to be fixed before readers are compared.

Reader rankings change with the dataset, so no single public benchmark is a reliable guide. MolNexTR trails MolGlyph on BioVista and collapses on JPO (53.0% against 80.0%) but leads it on USPTO (78.9% against 73.0%), a lead that comes from stereochemistry (Adranly, 2026). MolSight's paper reports 92% on USPTO, yet it read 70.9% of Patent300 crops and 45.2% of BioVista's, slightly below the older MolScribe (Jin, 2026). MolGlyph and MolScribe tie on Patent300 (78.6% and 78.3%) but differ by 32 points on journal-figure crops, and most of that gap is Markush structures (82.0% against 19.1%). BioVista was released by BioMiner's authors, so MolGlyph's lead there may partly be home ground; its lead on CLEF, UOB and JPO suggests it is not only that.

Every reader is weak on stereochemistry. None exceeds 51% on BioVista's chiral crops, and MolGlyph's chiral score rises from 50.8% to 77.7% when stereochemistry is ignored (Jin, 2026). Specialized models did not fix this: MolSight's stereochemistry checkpoint scored below its general one on every dataset, and MolGrapher's default model predicts no stereochemistry at all (Chhetri, 2026; Jin, 2026).

On the internal papers, the reader ranking holds, but the gap shrinks, because the losses move from reading to page structure. MolGlyph leads MolScribe by 32 points on BioVista, but finds only 10 more of the 220 internal molecules. Every system found all 17 molecules in paper 1, where each is drawn whole. Papers 2, 4 and 19 hold 198 of the 220 molecules, mostly as scaffolds whose substituents sit in a table or are drawn separately. The reader-only pipelines find 36 to 45 of them. BioMiner's language-model step is the only change that moved those papers: it raised paper 4 from 13 to 23 molecules by expanding R-group tables. Against BioMiner without that step, it cut the output from 166 to 108 SMILES, which is where its precision gain (38% to 68%) comes from (Daly, 2026).
conclusions: BioMiner is the strongest existing system we tested, but it finds only a third of the molecules in real papers. On the six internal papers, it found 73 of 220 molecules, and 68% of what it output was correct. The reader-only pipelines we ran found 54 to 64, with 31% to 39% of their output correct. The pipeline reported in the sponsor paper found 13 (Gulluoglu et al., 2026).

BioMiner's strengths come from two parts. Its reader, MolGlyph, was the best of seven readers on journal-figure crops (78%), stayed between 73% and 89% on six public datasets measured by two members, and is the only reader that handles R-group drawings well. BioMiner's language model removes junk output, and expands some R-group tables into full molecules. Finding the drawings is also largely solved: the detector BioMiner uses boxed 99.4% of the molecules on patent pages.

BioMiner's limitations are where most of the molecules are. In our papers, most molecules sit in scaffold-plus-R-group tables, or are drawn as separate pieces. BioMiner recovers only some of them: 23 of 104 in paper 19 and 9 of 34 in paper 2. Stereochemistry is weak in every reader we tested, MolGlyph included. BioMiner also needs a large GPU (its 32-billion-parameter model ran on one H200, 20 minutes for six papers); its GPU readings vary slightly with batch makeup, and some of its model weights are non-commercial, or carry no license.

BioVista is a sound test of reading, but not of extraction. Scores on it agree across our members' setups, and with the published numbers, but its crops are already cut out, hold one molecule each, and use one R-group notation that decides much of each reader's Markush score. MolGlyph reads 78% of its crops, but finds 29% of the molecules in our papers. For Phase 2, this means the next gains come from linking each scaffold to its table, and assembling full molecules, not from a better reader. A second reader is useful as an agreement check.
questions_intro: Each question comes from a result above.
questions: Which differences from the answer key should count as errors?

Exact match counts a molecule wrong if only its stereochemistry, tautomer or salt form differs. MolGlyph's chiral score rises from 51% to 78% when stereochemistry is ignored, paper 2's answer key lists one benzimidazole once as each tautomer, and paper 4's compound 18 is recorded as an HCl salt. For the way you would use the extracted structures, which of these differences matter, and which should we treat as the same molecule?
What balance of precision and recall would make the output useful?

BioMiner's output is 68% correct but covers 33% of the molecules, and our two-reader agreement check trades molecules for precision in the same way. How would you weigh a missed molecule against a wrong one in your downstream work?
How are R-group tables laid out in the literature you want to mine?

They hold most of the molecules every tool missed, and our papers already show three forms: substituents as table text (paper 19), drawn substituents (paper 2), and a series built from drawn pieces (paper 4). Which layouts are most common in the papers you care about, and what conventions, such as attachment-point labels, footnotes or tables split across pages, should we expect beyond these?
What should each extracted molecule carry besides its SMILES?

BioMiner links each structure to its compound label and activity values. Knowing which fields you need would tell us whether label linking is something to score or only a step toward assembly, and how you would want those links checked.
What would make a larger evaluation set most useful?

The six papers have already shaped our design, so they now serve as a development set. Which journals, chemistry areas, or document types (articles, patents, supplementary files) should a held-out test set cover, and are more of the intended 20 papers available with answer keys?
